chapter_theme: In the grove Manimekalai's companion Sudhamathi shows her its beauties; Udayakumaran, fresh from taming his maddened elephant, hears from a musician that she is there and comes for her; Sudhamathi locks her in the crystal pavilion and answers the prince's questions with a sermon on the body born of deeds, which the sight of the girl through the crystal outruns.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, newly turned from the courtesan's life
the Chola king's son, who desires Manimekalai
a merchant's son of Puhar, a yal player in the dancers' street
the prince's elephant, maddened by musth

manimekalai:4:1-18.reading: Sudhamathi points out the grove to Manimekalai as a stage: bees and beetles make music while a monkey watches a peacock dance, a royal swan sits on a lone lotus in a clear pool while a waterhen drums and a koel calls to another peacock, and a screw-pine's white pollen dusts a lotus as street dust dims the girl's own face.
manimekalai:4:1-18.nuance: The grove is described as a theatre (அரங்கு, முழவு, யாழ்), which keeps the courtesan's art in view at the moment Manimekalai has turned from it; the comparison at 15 (a lotus dulled by the dust of chariot streets like your face) quietly notes the grief that has worn her beauty, which Ettikumaran will also see.

manimekalai:4:19-26.unit_note: Boundary moved from 34 to 26: Sudhamathi's showing of the grove closes with காண்பழி at 26; lines 27 to 34 open the long sentence of the prince's elephant, which the core unit split from its main verb.
manimekalai:4:19-26.reading: Sudhamathi ends her tour with bees that mistake the girl's eyes for flowers and a kingfisher that dives at carp in a lotus pool and comes up hungry, and Manimekalai looks over the flowering garden.
manimekalai:4:19-26.nuance: The kingfisher that strikes and loses its prey (23 to 24) is set just before the prince enters the story; whether it is meant as a sign of his failed pursuit is a reading, not something the lines say.
manimekalai:4:19-26.event: Sudhamathi shows Manimekalai the grove and the pool, and Manimekalai looks at the garden.

manimekalai:4:27-46.unit_note: Boundary moved from 34 to 26 at the start and from 59 to 46 at the end: the elephant's rampage begins at 27 and its subduing ends with அடக்கி at 46, before the prince's chariot arrival at 47.
manimekalai:4:27-46.reading: The mount of the king's son Udayakumaran, the elephant Kalavegam, goes mad with musth, breaks free of its keepers like a storm-tossed ship that has lost mast and ropes, runs through the cowherds' street, the chariot street and the market and throws all Puhar into uproar, until the prince rides it down on a swift horse and quells its frenzy.
manimekalai:4:27-46.nuance: The syntax of 28 to 29 (உதயகுமரன் உரு கெழு மீது ஊர் மீயான்) is read here as the rider of the prince's own fearsome mount, so the elephant is his; the simile of the wrecked ship runs eight lines and the main verb comes only at 46. The deed echoes Kovalan's taming of a rogue elephant in the Silappathikaram.
manimekalai:4:27-46.event: The prince's elephant Kalavegam breaks loose in musth and rampages through Puhar; Udayakumaran overtakes it on horseback and subdues it.

manimekalai:4:47-60.unit_note: Boundary moved from 35 to 47 at the start and from 59 to 60 at the end: the prince's question begun at 59 closes with என்றலும் at 60.
manimekalai:4:47-60.reading: Holding the rail of his jewelled chariot, wearing the aar garland that alone shows he is not Murugan, the prince drives into the dancers' street and finds the merchant's son Ettikumaran lying with a woman on a flower bed by a window, his yal in his arms, still as a painted figure, and asks what trouble has struck him.
manimekalai:4:47-60.nuance: The ஆர் (aar) garland is the Chola emblem; the line makes the prince's beauty godlike and his lineage the only mark that tells him from the god. Ettikumaran's stillness is the courtesan quarter's music stopped.
manimekalai:4:47-60.event: Udayakumaran drives into the dancers' street and asks Ettikumaran, who sits frozen beside a woman with his yal, what has troubled him.

manimekalai:4:61-84.unit_note: Boundary moved from 60 to 61 at the start and from 83 to 84 at the end: Manimekalai's speech begun at 79 closes with என் செய்கு?' என at 84.
manimekalai:4:61-84.reading: Ettikumaran bows and says that seeing Manimekalai, Madhavi's daughter, entering the grove with her beauty faded like a flower kept in a casket, brought back the cruel grief of Kovalan, so that his hand slipped onto a jarring string; glad at the news, the prince says he will bring her back in his chariot and drives to the grove gate, and Manimekalai, hearing the chariot, recalls Vasanthamaalai telling Madhavi that Udayakumaran, through Chithirapathi, had set his heart on her, and asks what she should do.
manimekalai:4:61-84.nuance: Three voices meet here: Ettikumaran (65 to 71), the prince (73 to 74) and Manimekalai (79 to 84). The same sight moves the musician to grief for Kovalan and the prince to gladness; the merchant reads her faded beauty as mourning, the prince as a chance. Line 61 (வீங்கு இள முலையொடு) is read as Ettikumaran rising with the woman beside him; 69 to 70 (நீர்மையை நீக்கி வெம் பகை நரம்பின்) as grief driving the music out of his hand, and neither is sure.
manimekalai:4:61-84.event: Ettikumaran tells the prince that the sight of Manimekalai in the grove, recalling Kovalan's fate, threw his playing off; the prince drives to the grove to carry her off, and Manimekalai, hearing his chariot, asks Sudhamathi what to do.

manimekalai:4:85-104.unit_note: Boundary moved from 84 to 85 at the start and from 98 to 104 at the end: the prince's questions run from 95 to உரை? என at 104, across the core break at 98.
manimekalai:4:85-104.reading: Trembling like a peacock, Sudhamathi bids Manimekalai enter the crystal pavilion, bolts it with her inside and stands five bow-lengths off; the prince halts his chariot, sweeps the grove with his eyes and, finding her alone, asks whether the girl has grown to know her slender waist, whether her lisping speech has ripened and her teeth come in like pearls, whether her long eyes now speak of Kama, and why she has left the ascetics' dwelling to come here alone.
manimekalai:4:85-104.nuance: The prince's questions are a catalogue of a girl's coming of age in the stock images of love poetry, asked of a girl who has taken to the ascetics; his last question names exactly the change he does not accept (மாதவர் உறைவிடம் ஒரீஇ). Lines 89 to 90 (ஐ விலின் கிடக்கை) are read as Sudhamathi standing five bow-lengths from the pavilion, and 96 (உன் திறம் அறிந்தேன்) as the prince saying he knows who she is; both are doubtful.
manimekalai:4:85-104.event: Sudhamathi locks Manimekalai inside the crystal pavilion; the prince arrives and questions Sudhamathi about the girl's ripening and why she is there.

manimekalai:4:105-125.unit_note: Boundary moved from 99 to 105 at the start; the unit keeps Sudhamathi's whole answer (107 to 121) with the narration that frames it.
manimekalai:4:105-125.reading: Distressed as one shut in a closed room, Sudhamathi asks whether women must teach knowledge, worth and royal custom to the heir of the strong one who, ashamed of his youth, put on old age to give a verdict, and then tells him one thing: this human body is born of deeds and is the field where deeds ripen, flesh to be cast out once its finery is gone, bound to age and die, a seat of disease, a hold for attachment, a vessel of faults, a bed of anger like a snake in its anthill, holding sorrow, care, helplessness, lament and a restless mind; knowing it so, he should turn from it; but before her words reach his heart, the girl appears before him through the crystal like a coral doll.
manimekalai:4:105-125.nuance: The sermon is answered at once by the story: before it can reach him (123), the hiding place shows her body through the crystal, the very body she has just called flesh. Her opening is a modesty formula that is also a rebuke: the Chola who judged in youth (108) was wise without being told. The run of sorrows at 118 (அவலம் கவலை கையாறு அழுங்கல்) reads like the Buddhist list of griefs, but the unit names no school, so its claims are tagged general.
manimekalai:4:105-125.event: Sudhamathi tells the prince that the body is a karma-born thing of flesh, sickness and faults and urges him to turn from it; before her words take hold, Manimekalai's form shows through the crystal wall.

claims.claim: the human body comes from past deeds and is the place where deeds bear their fruit
stripped of its adornments the body is only flesh fit to be thrown out, subject to age, death and disease
one who knows the body for what it is should turn his back on it

links.note: The quatrain mocks the fool who calls a body of nine oozing openings 'broad-shouldered one'; Sudhamathi answers the prince's love-poetry questions about Manimekalai with the same inside-out view of the body.
links.teaches: The epic stages the quatrain's cure as speech to a lover just after he has used the love-poem epithets, and then shows it failing: the sight of the girl reaches him before the words do.

gains.a: Sudhamathi's catalogue is placed in an existing ethics genre that answers love poetry's epithets one by one.
gains.b: The quatrain's sure contempt for the fool gets a test case in which the cure is spoken in time and still loses to sight.

links.note: Pattinattar calls the body the enjoyment of deeds, gone the moment deeds end, and sends the mind to Siva's feet; Sudhamathi calls it born of deeds and the field where they ripen, and asks only that it be known and turned from.
links.teaches: The two share the premise that the body exists to eat karma but part on the remedy: the Saiva poet needs Siva's feet, while the epic's speaker names no god and puts release in seeing the body truly.

gains.a: Sudhamathi's godless remedy stands out once set beside a Saiva statement of the same premise.
gains.b: Pattinattar's appeal to Siva's feet is shown to be an addition to a premise that a Buddhist epic holds without it.

links.note: The proverb verse tells of the young Chola who tied on grey hair and judged a case (உரைமுடிவு) to prove that a family's craft comes half-known; Sudhamathi names the same act (உரை முடிவு காட்டிய உரவோன்) to shame his heir.
links.teaches: The proverb says the line's judgment is inborn, and the epic turns the same story against the line's heir, who must be lectured by a woman, so the inherited craft is invoked because it is missing.

gains.a: The allusion at 108 is fixed to a known story whose point is wisdom in youth, which sharpens Sudhamathi's rebuke of a youth acting unwisely.
gains.b: The proverb's claim that a family's craft comes by birth meets a heir of the same line who lacks it.

links.note: Kaathai 3 says the crystal pavilion lets no voice out but shows the body outside (விளிப்பு அறைபோகாது மெய் புறத்து இடூஉம்); Sudhamathi hides Manimekalai in it.
links.teaches: The hiding place was announced as one that hides speech but shows the body, so the shelter Sudhamathi picks is the one that will display the girl to the prince while she preaches against the body.

links.note: Manimekalai hears the prince's chariot with fear and asks what to do; in the next kaathai, after he has gone, she confesses that her heart followed the stranger who had scorned her.
links.teaches: The crystal wall kept her body from his hands but not her heart from him, so the flight here and the confession after it show the girl's renunciation is not yet secure.

links.note: Kovalan tamed a rogue elephant that had seized an old Brahmin; his daughter's pursuer Udayakumaran tames his own elephant gone mad in Puhar.
links.teaches: The father's deed of rescue returns as the prince's feat of strength on his way to chase the daughter, so the same heroic act is shown serving compassion once and desire the second time.

source_issues: Line 97: a closing quotation mark stands after முலை in the middle of the prince's speech, which runs on to உரை? என at 104, where no closing mark appears.
Line 1 opens with a quotation mark for Sudhamathi's speech carried over from the previous kaathai, with no speaker named until line 25.
Line 125 ends with a bare என், the kaathai's closing particle, so the last sentence reads as cut short in this text.
